evidence.claim: Western Skies follows rolling hills and ridge tops through western Iowa, linking working farmsteads and rural towns.
evidence.quote: Iowa’s landscapes of rolling hills, working farmsteads, and tranquil small town life.

evidence.claim: The paved, 142-mile byway parallels Interstate 80 and connects with Interstate 29.
evidence.quote: The 142-mile Western Skies Scenic Byway parallels Interstate 80 and joins Interstate 29

evidence.claim: Golden Hills RC&D, its coordinating organization, presents the drive as a journey through Iowa’s agricultural past and cultural heritage.
evidence.quote: the Western Skies Scenic Byway offers both while showcasing Iowa’s agricultural past and cultural heritage.

evidence.claim: Its suggested itineraries span one or two days.
evidence.quote: Choose your adventure on a one- to two-day itinerary on Western Skies Scenic Byway!

evidence.claim: paved
evidence.quote: SURFACE: Paved

evidence.claim: its coordinating organization
evidence.quote: The Western Skies Scenic Byway is coordinated by S eth Brooks at Golden Hills RC&D

evidence.claim: Dedicated in 1998, Western Skies was among Iowa’s first state-designated scenic byways.
evidence.quote: The Western Skies Scenic Byway , dedicated in 1998, is among the first state-designated scenic byways in Iowa.

evidence.claim: The designation gathered 14 rural towns across Harrison, Shelby, Audubon and Guthrie counties into one corridor.
evidence.quote: The Byway is 142 miles long, traveling through Harrison, Shelby, Audubon and Guthrie Counties, including 14 rural towns.

evidence.claim: Those towns include Westphalia, founded in 1872 by German Catholic farmers and small merchants, and Elk Horn, where a Danish folk school drew immigrants beginning in 1878.
evidence.quote: Westphalia was founded in 1872 as a colony of German Catholic farmers and small merchants.

evidence.claim: Elk Horn, where a Danish folk school drew immigrants beginning in 1878.
evidence.quote: This school, founded in 1878 by Danish immigrant Kristian Ostergaard, was the first Danish folk school in America. It served as a magnet for Danish immigrants, drawing them to Elk Horn in great numbers.

evidence.claim: Start near Missouri Valley on Highway 30, then choose Highway 44 or the northern loop through Woodbine and County Road F32; both reach Harlan.
evidence.quote: Taking Highway 30 east from Missouri Valley, travelers have the option to turn east onto State Highway 44 or to continue north into Woodbine where the byway forms a loop at County Road F32. Both routes lead travelers to Harlan

evidence.claim: Continue east to Kimballton, with Elk Horn on a southbound Highway 173 spur.
evidence.quote: A spur of the Byway runs south from Kimballton on Highway 173 through Elk Horn and on to Interstate 80.

evidence.claim: Back on Highway 44, the rolling ridge top leads through Hamlin and Guthrie Center to Panora, where P28 turns south to Stuart.
evidence.quote: Back on Highway 44, follow the rolling ridge top through Hamlin and Guthrie Center, and into Panora. Turning south on to P28, the byway ends at Stuart

evidence.claim: Westphalia began in 1872 as a colony of German Catholic farmers and small merchants.
evidence.quote: Westphalia was founded in 1872 as a colony of German Catholic farmers and small merchants.

evidence.claim: They named it for Germany’s Province of Westphalia.
evidence.quote: It was named after the Province of Westphalia, in Germany.

evidence.claim: The town’s German heritage is visible in a church built by its founders, one of the architectural features Travel Iowa highlights along this route.
evidence.quote: German heritage is also evident in the towns of Westphalia and Panama where you will see architecturally stunning German churches, built with great care and craftsmanship by town founders.

evidence.claim: Elk Horn’s Danish connections run through education as well as its working windmill.
evidence.quote: Elk Horn was also the site of the Elk Horn Højskole.

evidence.claim: In 1878, Danish immigrant Kristian Ostergaard founded the Elk Horn Højskole, America’s first Danish folk school.
evidence.quote: This school, founded in 1878 by Danish immigrant Kristian Ostergaard, was the first Danish folk school in America.

evidence.claim: The school attracted Danish immigrants, and in 1894 its owner, Pastor Kristian Anker, sold it to the Danish Lutheran Church in North America for a seminary and college.
evidence.quote: In 1894, Pastor Kristian Anker, then owner and principal of the Elk Horn Højskole, sold it to the newly formed Danish Lutheran Church in North America for use as a seminary and college.

evidence.claim: The seminary moved to Nebraska in 1896.
evidence.quote: In 1896,  the seminary was relocated and consolidated with Trinity Seminary at Dana College in Blair, Nebraska.

evidence.claim: Elk Horn now houses the Museum of Danish America and a working Danish windmill.
evidence.quote: Elk Horn is known as an enclave of Danish ethnicity and is home to the Museum of Danish America.

evidence.claim: The school attracted Danish immigrants
evidence.quote: It served as a magnet for Danish immigrants, drawing them to Elk Horn in great numbers.

evidence.claim: a working Danish windmill.
evidence.quote: Elk Horn is now home to the only working Danish windmill in America.

evidence.claim: Stuart grew with the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad in the late 1860s.
evidence.quote: Stuart got its start in the late 1860s, following construction of the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad through the territory.

evidence.claim: Captain Charles Stuart helped bring the railroad here and founded the city that carries his name.
evidence.quote: It is named for Captain Charles Stuart, who was instrumental in bringing the railroad to the city and also founded the city itself.

evidence.claim: The settlement was platted in 1870 and incorporated in 1887.
evidence.quote: The settlement was platted on September 29, 1870 and on February 6, 1887, Stuart was officially incorporated.

evidence.claim: Its railroad connection is represented on the National Register of Historic Places by the Stuart Passenger Station, dated 1869.
evidence.quote: Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad: Stuart Passenger Station (1869)

evidence.claim: The byway ends here, at the town where Bonnie and Clyde staged their last bank robbery.
evidence.quote: At the other end of the byway, you’ll find a bit of infamous history in Stuart where Bonnie and Clyde staged their last bank robbery.

evidence.claim: on the National Register of Historic Places
evidence.quote: Four buildings in town are listed on the National Register of Historic Places:

evidence.claim: Travel Iowa points to German churches in Westphalia and Panama and the Danish villages of Elk Horn and Kimballton as expressions of that heritage along the route.
evidence.quote: German heritage is also evident in the towns of Westphalia and Panama

evidence.claim: the Danish villages of Elk Horn and Kimballton
evidence.quote: located in the Danish villages of Elk Horn and Kimballtown.

evidence.claim: The western loop and Elk Horn spur offer different branches of the drive before the route’s eastern finish at Interstate 80.
evidence.quote: Turning south on to P28, the byway ends at Stuart, located along Interstate 80 at exit 93.

evidence.claim: Danish cooking remains part of the town’s life, with businesses making and selling Danish bakery goods.
evidence.quote: Danish cuisine is made in Elk Horn, and the community has businesses selling Danish bakery goods.

evidence.claim: The town’s former All Saints Catholic Church and Masonic Temple Building are also listed on the National Register.
evidence.quote:
The former All Saints Catholic Church (1910)
Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific Railroad: Stuart Passenger Station (1869)
Masonic Temple Building (1894)

flags: Road history is limited to dedication in 1998; cache identifies no builders or designation campaign.
Westphalia is shorter than 90 words because its cache offers little beyond settlement and the founder-built church; no architectural details or access invented.
Elk Horn naming accounts conflict within 06.txt: creek derivation versus Caroline Whitney Winters’s elk-antler explanation. Both omitted.
Official 142-mile route includes loops and a spur; material maps 133.3 miles. Do not treat 142 miles as a single end-to-end drive.
Travel Iowa spells Kimballton as Kimballtown once; the byway coordinator and dedicated cached articles consistently use Kimballton.
